content:
Hi! I'm starting a master's thesis in Formal Methods (due June 2027, September at the latest) and I'm settling on a topic. One part of it should be a Lean formalization of a reasonably substantial theorem that isn't in mathlib yet. My supervisors and I picked differential geometry, since that's where I'm most comfortable in mathlib after contributing to quotient manifolds.

Cartan's closed subgroup theorem is on the 1000 theorems list, doesn't seem to be in mathlib, and I couldn't find a stated intention to formalize it. A preliminary look suggests it's doable with some work, but I'm not an expert on the topic and my supervisors aren't mathlib contributors, so I'd like an outside opinion.

  1. Is anyone already working on this, or on something close enough that I'd be duplicating effort?
  2. Is a year realistic? My rough sense is that the main missing pieces are a Lie product (and a Trotter formula), the exponential map for Lie groups (I think this might have some relation with @Winston Yin (尹維晨) 's work), and some notion of embedded submanifold (which I think would depend on some of Samantha Guevara's work supervised by @Michael Rothgang). But this is a preliminary impression, I haven't worked through a proof in detail.
  3. Is this something mathlib actually wants? If there's something more useful I could work on in this area instead, I'd be glad to hear it. In general I'm very open to changing topic.

For context on the "not already in mathlib" constraint: my bachelor's thesis was a proof of Urysohn's lemma, which helped me learn a lot, but this was already in mathlib, so now it's just sitting there in a repo. This time I'd like to upstream the work if possible (though I dont need to upstream everything during the thesis, I could keep working on it afterwards).

Other parts of the thesis will look at type theory (with some Lean formalizations of related CS concepts) and at synthetic differential geometry, possibly with an eye to Lean. I'm aware of Riccardo Brasca's recent work on this; I do not know yet exactly how this will look like though.

Pepa Montero Jimena said:

One part of it should be a Lean formalization of a reasonably substantial theorem that isn't in mathlib yet

How about the Weierstrass–Enneper parameterisation?

Are you aware of work towards Cartan's closed subgroup theorem in Tau Ceti? Do you care? I am personally interested in having a formal proof of Cartan's closed subgroup theorem in a timely manner (before February, say), so that I can fully formalise my non-formalisation paper which uses it.

In general, at this point "do you care if there has been some formalization of your topic already" (which may not be of mathlib's quality) becomes a salient question. For virtually any topic X, you can produce a formalisation rather quickly now by just pointing an AI at it. (That usually doesn't teach you a lot, though.)

Jeremy Tan said:

How about the Weierstrass–Enneper parameterisation?

I will take a look at this, thanks!

FWIW, I view contributing to mathlib (even of content that's already in Tau Ceti) as valuable --- the point of this process is gaining insight into how to formalise things best, into the mathematics, improving the surrounding infrastructure, etc. I've seen several examples where the Tau Ceti formalisation is not ideal, and mathlib can and should do better. To "just get any formalization", an AI library is the shorter path.

Re: synthetic differential geometry
My impression is that this is a fairly niche topic, rather disconnected from mainstream research. Of course, that need not stop you - but if your goal is to produce something more broadly considered interesting, I would advise against that part.

@Yaël Dillies Yes this seems to be in a Tau Ceti roadmap. I hadn't seen it before but I had no doubt it would start being worked on before I had a chance to finish myself haha. I had discussed this with my supervisors and we all agree it's not very important for us. This is not an autoformalization project for me

Michael Rothgang said:

the point of this process is gaining insight into how to formalise things best, into the mathematics, improving the surrounding infrastructure, etc

This is the main goal for me and my supervisors as well. The recent FLT formalization came up and this was essentially what they said

Michael Rothgang said:

Re: synthetic differential geometry

Thank you for your thoughts! For now the idea is to focus on reading a lot about HoTT, we'll see from there :)

@Yaël Dillies Another thing is that I'm not sure about the "before February" part :sweat_smile:, apart from whether or not I could do it this fast, I believe this project would depend on other projects that also may not have finished by then. Tau Ceti might be faster though

Thank you for the replies. The reason I am asking about Tau Ceti and completion date is that I would rank the possible situations at the time I defend my licentiate thesis (PhD midpoint, between February and July for me) from worst to best as follows:

  1. I formalise my paper modulo the Lie theory prerequisites (Cartan, but also Duhamel's formula).
  2. I formalise my paper fully, but the Lie theory prerequisites are horrible slop proofs.
  3. I formalise my paper fully, but the Lie theory prerequisites are in Tau Ceti.
  4. I formalise my paper fully and the prerequisites are in mathlib.
  5. I formalise my paper fully and most of it has made its way to mathlib.

If Tau Ceti gets Cartan formalised, then I can easily aim for 3 (Duhamel is already in Tau Ceti). If you complete your project before February, then 4 is doable. If you finish it earlier or I help you finish and upstream, then I could possibly reach 5.

Looking at timelines (Yael defending between Feb and July, Pepa finishing between July and September), "finish before February" seems a bit ambitious. (Though I like aiming for 4 or 5, just on a feasible time scale :-))

Pepa Montero Jimena said:

  1. Is this something mathlib actually wants?

Can't speak for the maintainers, but I would think yes. Cartan's closed subgroup theorem is an important classical result in Lie theory and used in many papers. I see no reason why it shouldn't be included in Mathlib.

Michael Rothgang said:

"finish before February" seems a bit ambitious.

Yeah, I am unsure that I can compromise to that! But I can start working on it and then reasess in a couple of months.
